messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq is a nineteen-year-old man of Jordanian descent who presents for an initial psychological assessment accompanied by his wife, though he asks to be seen alone. He works as an environmental scientist at a regional water-quality monitoring agency, a role he began only months ago, and he carries himself with a careful, watchful stillness that his supervisor has already noticed and quietly remarked upon. His PCL-5 score of 36 places him in the clinical range, and the picture that emerges across the first two sessions is one shaped decisively by years of physical abuse at the hands of his father during childhood.

Tariq describes a home environment defined by unpredictability and violence. His father's anger could arrive without warning — a raised voice that escalated within seconds into blows, a hand seizing him by the collar during what had seemed like an ordinary dinner. Arguments in the household were not conversations that might resolve; they were the opening movements of something dangerous. Being touched without warning — a hand on the shoulder, a sudden grip — had so reliably preceded pain that his nervous system came to treat any unexpected physical contact as an announcement of what was coming. Crying, whether his own or someone else's, had often preceded or accompanied the worst episodes, and the sound had become threaded with dread in ways he could not easily explain. These three experiences — arguments, unexpected touch, and the sound or sight of someone crying — remain the most potent triggers in his present life, each one capable of pulling him back into the texture of those childhood moments with an immediacy he finds frightening.

When any of these triggers arise now, Tariq's body responds as though the threat is current and physical. He becomes hypervigilant almost instantly, scanning the environment for danger. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels like common sense rather than symptom, that he is only safe when his back is against a wall and the room is visible to him. At work, where his team gathers in an open-plan office, he arrived on his first day and quietly repositioned his desk chair so that no one could approach him from behind. He studies his colleagues' faces with an attention they occasionally find unnerving — watching for the micro-expressions, the jaw tension, the shift in posture that he learned in childhood to read as warnings. Safe seating is not a preference but a requirement; in the field, when the team stops for lunch at a picnic table or a diner booth, he will circle the space before sitting, choosing the position from which he can see the most and be approached from the fewest directions. This persistent threat monitoring, once activated by a trigger, does not easily switch off — it sustains and amplifies his sense of danger, so that ordinary social interactions in the workplace feel laden with potential harm, and he leaves the office most evenings more wound up than when he arrived.

The hypervigilance, in turn, has shaped his behaviour in ways that have accumulated into a significantly restricted life. Threat monitoring has led him to organise his days around avoidance: he routes himself away from any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, including team meetings where decisions are contested. He avoids being alone in a room or building — paradoxically, because solitude removes the protective scanning of others' faces, leaving him without the early-warning system he depends on — and yet he also avoids people, pulling back from social contact that might unpredictably generate the very triggers he fears. These strategies, while offering momentary relief, have created their own trap: his avoidance of people and conflict has left him isolated at work, which means he encounters unfamiliar colleagues and unexpected interactions more frequently, not less, and these encounters are precisely the conditions in which arguments, sudden touch, or visible distress are most likely to arise. His wife has noticed that he will not sit with his back to the kitchen when they eat together, and that he flinches if she reaches for him without first speaking.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when a colleague placed a hand on his shoulder to congratulate him, and he spun around with his fists raised before he had any conscious thought. He was not hurt, and neither was his colleague, but the look on the man's face — startled, uncertain — stayed with him. What he most fears is that he will hurt someone who means him no harm. What he most hopes for, he says quietly, is to stop living as though his father is still in the room.
